coverage.assessment: Rome sequence: the revision drops the hinges that make the argument move. These are the Church's Cross as the force to follow, cheap fetish versus costly machine, the Cross's failure, and the Civitas Dei as the new attraction (F1, F3). The vicious circle, Alaric and Augustine still stand.
'This method' (p23) has lost its Baconian antecedent (F4). 'Both sides' in the boxing-match has lost its pagan champion (F2). Ara Coeli and Constantine's dates are intact.
Quoted speech is intact and correctly attributed: the Edict as an 'Act of Congress,' In hoc signo vinces, Augustine's questions, St. Louis's prayer and the Bacon maxim.

313, the year before, 410 and 430 are intact. 'For convenience' (p3), 'rather recklessly' and 'probably' survive. The self-deprecating hedge on the antique momentum was cut, so the economies claim now reads flatly (F5).
The final paragraph still points to a needed formula of acceleration without stating it. Adams's breakdown at Ara Coeli remains retrospective and third-person.

V1–V8 are verbatim and the commercial irony of p12 is intact. The dragging and resistance imagery (fish on a hook, the individual's unwitting insistence) is thinned (F7). The spider-versus-man contrast is flattened (F8).

The 'oldest theory' admission has lost its reason: Church, State, theology and philosophy all preached it. That weakens 'religion, philosophy, and science … hand in hand' (F6). Byzantium is reduced to 'forces not quite the same'; this is acceptable compression.
All three dependencies are intact at both endpoints in this run's drafts (008, 007, 027).

findings.claim: The revision cuts two hinges that the first draft kept. The first is the Church-paragraph opening, where the dynamic theory accepts the Church's Cross as 'the force that attracts.' The p12 Constantine passage now follows 'economize the gods' without that frame. The second is the comparison with hiring occult force instead of building machines, so 'cheap' in p14 has no comparison point.
findings.counterevidence: 'Economize the gods' and 'Trust of State Religions' still imply the economic reading, and the p12 satire stays intelligible.

evidence.quote: The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.
All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts. The Church points out this force in the Cross
Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker
no one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.
Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point. Outside of it, the Roman world was incredibly poor.

findings.minimal_repair: Prefix p12 with 'All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts. The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.' Then open p14 with the source's 'no one could afford … trifling expense' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: required (the essential section on Rome's fall, Constantine's trust and slave and fetish)
findings.reader_effect: The Constantine satire and the slave/fetish economics read as assertions. They should read as the dynamic theory applying its method of assigning values to attracting forces.
findings.title: Rome argument loses its 'follow the Cross' step and its machine-versus-fetish rationale

findings.claim: The first draft had already dropped 'to decide a final test of force between the divine powers.' The revision also cuts Eugene's raising of Hercules. 'Society on both sides' now watches a match in which only the Cross is named, so the contest of gods behind 'bet on the gods' disappears.
findings.counterevidence: 'Rival' and 'both sides' still signal two parties. The plan allows Theodosius/Eugene to be trimmed.

evidence.quote: and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match, to decide a final test of force between the divine powers.
and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.
Theodosius marched against his rival Eugene with the Cross for physical champion; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'and Eugene raised the image of Hercules to fight for the pagans;' (about 12 words), or cut the Theodosius sentence entirely.
findings.plan_relation: optional tradeoff, but a trimmed version must not leave a dangling 'both sides'
findings.reader_effect: The image collapses into a human rivalry. The joke that the pagan and Christian divine powers are being tested like fighters is lost.
findings.title: Boxing-match left with only one champion

findings.claim: Three linked statements were cut by the revision; the first draft kept all three. The first is that society felt the Cross had failed to protect its Church. The second is that the Civitas Dei became the new sum of attraction with the same mechanical weakness. The third is that the new forces dropped 'at the precise moment' of the Civitas Dei's triumph. The 'outcry' and 'Yet the attraction remained constant' lose their causes. The compass/gunpowder passage also loses its irony.
findings.counterevidence: 'Against the Cross' implies disappointment. 'Civitas Dei' still recurs in p15 and p20.

evidence.quote: felt still more deeply the disappointment in its new power, the Cross, which had failed to protect its Church.
The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics
The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics that had wrecked the Civitas Romae.
The outcry against the Cross became so loud among Christians that Bishop Augustine of Hippo was led to write a famous treatise
at the precise moment when the Cross on one side and the Crescent on the other, proclaimed the complete triumph of the Civitas Dei.
the sudden, unexplained appearance of at least two new natural forces of the highest educational value in mechanics.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the source's 'The Civitas Dei, in its turn … wrecked the Civitas Romae.' Then append to p17 the source's 'Literally, these two forces … triumph of the Civitas Dei.'
findings.plan_relation: required (the essential sections on Augustine and on the compass and gunpowder)
findings.reader_effect: The thread the argument later relies on is thinned. That thread is the Civitas Dei as the force that Luther and the Puritans try to restore and that the new forces later displace.
findings.title: Civitas Dei chain broken: the Cross's failure, the new attraction, and the ironic timing of compass and gunpowder

findings.claim: The revision cuts two things. One is the individual's unwitting insistence, which sets up the Gutenberg-to-Puritans series. The other is 'Europe saw itself, violently resisting … as a fish caught on a hook.' 'Europe's resistance' is then presupposed rather than shown.
findings.counterevidence: 'As mechanical as the fall of a feather' and 'dragged and drove Europe' still convey involuntariness.

evidence.quote: Europe saw itself, violently resisting, wrenched into false positions, drawn along new lines as a fish that is caught on a hook

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'Europe saw itself, violently resisting, drawn along new lines as a fish that is caught on a hook' before the resistance sentence.
findings.reader_effect: The section on acceleration after 1500 keeps its claims but loses the comic-pathetic image of society hooked and dragged.
findings.title: Imagery of involuntary dragging and resistance thinned

findings.claim: Two cuts were made. 'Man had in the beginning no power of analysis or synthesis approaching that of the spider' is reduced to 'Man had acute sensibility.' 'With little or no effort on his part, all these forces formed his thought' is removed. The paragraph thus loses its turn and its closing inversion.
findings.counterevidence: V2 in p2 already states the inversion that forces capture man.

evidence.quote: Man had in the beginning no power of analysis or synthesis approaching that of the spider, or even of the honey-bee;
With little or no effort on his part, all these forces formed his thought, induced his action, and even shaped his figure.
Man had acute sensibility to the higher forces. Fire taught him secrets that no other animal could learn;

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the final 'With little or no effort …' sentence.
findings.reader_effect: The early teachers remain, but the paradox of a feeble analyst with acute sensibility, shaped without effort, is weakened.
findings.title: Spider image loses its man-versus-spider contrast and its payoff

strengths: All eight protected excerpts appear verbatim, including the stock-broker reading of the Edict as an 'Act of Congress' and the bet on the gods as on a horse.
Dates (313, the year before, 410, towards 430) and the attribution of the Augustine quotation are exact.
The spider's 'fatal mistakes,' the early teachers (fire, water, animals, grains) and the triad 'Susceptibility … highest educator' are preserved.
The St. Louis/Greek fire scene and 'gunpowder and the Cross' keep their comic timing.
The final paragraph is intact; it calls for a 'mechanical formula of acceleration' without stating it, handing off cleanly to 036.
summary: The revision keeps every protected excerpt, all three dependencies, the dates, the Augustine attribution, the surviving hedges and the forward-pointing close. The problems are thinned connectives rather than outright breaks. Several argument hinges were cut in the revision: the Church/Cross 'follow the force' step, the machine-versus-fetish comparison, the Civitas Dei becoming the new sum of attraction, Bacon's method before 'this method,' and the explanation of why the theory is 'oldest.' The Theodosius/Eugene contest now has only one champion. None of these is a blocker, but each warrants a small restoration.
